Messages.Author: Ector
Messages.Body:
AFAIK, the current rulings about PTW sound like this:

* A player must try to achieve GW if he has reasonable chances to get
it.
* If the player has no reasonable chances to get GW, he must try to get
the maximum number of VPs (i.e. 2VPs if he has reasonable chances to
get them, or 1VP otherwise).

In my playgroup we frequently stumble on the following situation: when
some players start to negotiate about a table-splitting deal, the other
players quickly determine that WITH THAT DEAL active they won't be able
to get any VPs. So, they are trying to get included into that deal,
even for 1VP.
Such behaviour leads to extremely stupid games where three players
quickly kill the remaining two and split the rewards. I wonder, whether
such behaviour is legal or not? I mean, if two players are really
unable to get GW and trying to split the table, should we count the
threat of the NOT-YET-MADE deal as a reason for the third player to
give up the GW or 2VP? The 2-2-1 deals really became a menace for us.

Thanks in advance,
Ector

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:


Sounds fine, so long as the NOT-YET-MADE deal was legal in the first
place (that is, you have to wait until one of the two instigators is
really out of the running for a GW before the process can start).

It seems likely that the player who's taking the losing end of the
initial deal would have a better outcome by dealing with one of the
other players instead, of course.

Or the three other players could also make their own deal (excluding
the two instigators), instead of rewarding the instigators, as well.

Here is my question about this. Why are people making such deals in
what is presumably casual play (i.e. non tournament play, where no one
is playing for money and no one is keeping track of VPs for any purpose
other than bragging rights. And maybe a beer.) Like, I am generally
fundamentally opposed to table splitting deals in any situation in
VTES, competition or no. But at least in a competetive play situation,
where you are playing for money (money being code for "prizes of some
type") and game wins/VPs are being kept track of for purposes of
winning money and or getting rating points (assuming you care about
such things), I can understand why people broker and accept such deals.
Personally, I rarely have anything to do with such deals, and generally
actively try and undermine such deals when other people make them
(although I have been known to, in the end game when there is only me
and another guy, bargain to mutually withdraw rather than fight it out
to the bitter end). But at least I understand where they come from.

Now I may be misunderstanding you, and this question may come from the
context of a tournament. But if not, why are people making such deals?
Isn't it best for everyone, in such play situations, to simply play the
game, see if you win or lose, and if you win, great, if you lose, ok,
and in either case, just play another game?

Like, this is in no way a criticism, but I'm trying to understand other
people's play groups, I guess--like my local play group, when playing
"casually" (i.e. we are having a general play night of VTES with
nothing on the line), no one ever makes any deals at all other than the
general quid pro quo kinda "hey, rescue my guy from torpor and I'll
help you pass your next vote" deal. Likely, no one would ever consider
brokering a table split deal.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Matthew T. Morgan
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 26 May 2006, LSJ wrote:

> Or the three other players could also make their own deal (excluding
> the two instigators), instead of rewarding the instigators, as well.

This works. It's a great way to break up a table split deal. In fact, if
the three non-instigating players are on the ball and can do simple math
(3 vs. 2), early table split deals should never work.

Ector, if you like I can furnish you with an anecdote or two, but you can
probably imagine how it works. Next time you see one of these table
splits, suggest to the other players they form an alliance to break up the
split. The original instigators will quickly backpedal and the deal will
often become so confused that people just go back to plan A: bleed prey.

By the way, a deal that results in 2:2:1 can only be legal if all three of
those players have no chance of a game win. How often can that really
happen?

Matt Morgan

Hello everyone! I'm from the same playgroup as Ector's.

I want to ask LSJ about the detail explanation and interpretation of
the rules quoted above, because we faced with some situations when it
took place a table-splitting in the FINAL play of the tournament. There
are some players that understand this rule exactly as it is and don't
make any exceptions for the final game (and what is important, the
judge shares this opinion). So when somebody concludes that Game Win is
unreachable for him he initiate the table-splitting in order to receive
at least one or two Victory Points (I'll be damned if I know what for!
In final, VP without GW is useless). He motivates those deal with the
mentioned rules - "I can't reach GW so I'll maximize my VP". Judge
accept this deal. Of course, the others have no choice but to make
another table-splitting deal and game quickly collapse into
confrontation of two quasi-commands...or, if the first player made
2-2-1 deal with two players, another two players quickly lose the game.

Please, explain to me, is it normal? Do everyone should seek for the
table-splitting (and destabilize the game) if the chance of receiving
GW is minor? Is it legal for him to give away that minor chance and try
to receive at least a couple of VPs even in final game?

train how to make a counter-deal against other players dealing.

player plays more than one deck in that situation. And even in that
games we deal. That goes like: "The Brujah deck would offer a 3-1 deal
to his Ventrue predator. " "No, he would not like that the Brujahs get
the GW. So he would only accept a 2-2 deal." "But then the Nosferatu
would offer the Ventrue a 2-3 deal before he get killed by the Brujah."

You are right that it can sometimes irritate newbies. But they usually
learn fast. And should they learn dealing for the first time at a
tournament?

Matthew T. Morgan wrote:
> If dealing is the path to GW or maximized VPs, then that's what is expected.

Heh. Thinking about it more, I realized where some of my not
understanding table split deals in non tournament play comes
from--incentive, or lack therof. Like, in competetive play, there is
incentive to maximize VPs, even if you lose the game, as snaring an
extra VP or some tournament points or whatever by virtue of taking the
losing end of a table split deal can be significant. Everyone has
incentive to deal, even for a losing deal.

In non tournament (i.e. casual) play, there is no incentive to accept
the losing end of the deal, really (other than, ya know, making the
game end, but you could just as easily make the game end by going down
fighting). In a tournament, you can look at your position and say "I
figure I have a less than 20% chance of winning from here. I might as
well make a deal that pays off, even if I don't win.", and then make a
deal for a few VPs and help someone else win. In casual play, as it
doesn't matter if you lose or win in either direction, you have much
less incentive to make that deal and much more of a reason to try for
the unlikely victory--yeah, you might have an 80% chance of losing, but
if you win, it'd be cool, so you might as well try, as you have, ya
know, nothing to lose by trying for the risky/unlikely win.

-Peter

Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com
Messages.Body:
x5m...@gmx.de wrote:
> Peter, it looks like you think dealing is absolutely random and has no
> connection with the game. But that is wrong; good VP splitting deals
> depend absolutely on an analysis of the game state.

Nah. I don't think it is random. I just think that unless there is
actual incentive to be on the losing end of the deal (i.e. getting the
VP you wouldn't have otherwise, which makes a difference in tournament
play but not so much in casual play), there is no reason to accept it.
And if there is no reason to accept the losing end of the deal, there
can't be a table split deal.

To make a table split deal, one guy has to convince someone else at the
table to help him win. In competetive play, the tangible payoff of
being the stooge in that deal is not insignificant (getting 2VPs
instead of 0VPs can be very important in a 3R tournament, say). Without
the long term consequence in casual play, there is no incentive to help
someone else win, as you are better off trying for the risky and
unlikely win rather than dealing to be the stooge, as the incentive to
pull off an unlikely but exciting game win (or whatever) seems like a
much more tangible incenitve than making a losing deal with no actual
incentive.

> So you also have to
> train them and see what happens. You have to train what is a rationale
> deal and how you can get him through psychological. And you can also
> train how to make a counter-deal against other players dealing.

But you are training in a false environment--with no money on the line,
no actual tournament win to be had, the deal making is irrational. In a
tournament, there are stakes that make dealing make sense. In casual
play, even if you are pretending there are stakes, they aren't there.

Like when you are playing poker for no actual money, there is no
incentive to not make risky low percentage win bets or gambles, as you
got nothing to actually lose.

> You are right that it can sometimes irritate newbies. But they usually
> learn fast. And should they learn dealing for the first time at a
> tournament?

I think a lot of this has to do with the overall validity of dealing vs
not dealling. As I have mentioned before, I don't tend to make table
split deals in competition, and tend to discourage/sabotage them as
often as possible in competition, as I find excessive dealmaking to be
irksome (it slows the game down and turns it far more into kingmaker
than I am fond of), to the point that I'm generally willing to lose
rather than help someone else win. But that is me.

Like, I don't think newbies need to learn dealing at all, as they can
do just fine without dealmaking. That being said, again, I can see how
deals like this work in competetive play, but without the incentive
built in, I find it weird that it takes place in casual play.

-Peter

NO. Convincing can be part of dealing like bluffing can be part of
combat or bleeding. But dealing with good players is analysing the game
state and defining, what is the best part for every player.

Example (a real one): Four player table. A is the strongest. B is about
to die. C (!Malkavian ie. crosstable power) is about to die, the
question is, will he die by A or B. D (thats me) plays wall, so has
problems to oust A but can wall up and defend very well. D offers B and
C a 2-1-1 deal. The deal is absolutely rationale: B and C will not be
able to get 1 VP without a deal. A offers in that situation a deal to C
3-1. C has to decide was is the best deal for him. Both deals give him
1 VP, so he thinks the deal of A is better, because A is the strongest
player. B dies. D is able to wall up and the game goes in the time out.
So A1,5, B 0, C 0,5, D 0,5 VPs. It looks like C made the false
decision, but that was his analysis not that he was convinced.

> But you are training in a false environment--with no money on the line,
> no actual tournament win to be had, the deal making is irrational. In a
> tournament, there are stakes that make dealing make sense. In casual
> play, even if you are pretending there are stakes, they aren't there.

Is it irrational to play for ousting your prey and getting VPs in
casual games? You could instead attack the player who won the last risk
game, play to be a absolutely weird Malkavian or throw your cards in
the air when you start losing. Playing is about accepting rules that
are set by a different world (the game world) and ignoring the rules of
the real world. If i can accept the rule to oust my prey, i can also
accept to play to absolutely win, i.e. make the most GWs and if that is
not possible the most VPs, even by dealing.

BTW, its nice to dicuss game philosophy with you, because you have such
a different view.

Frank

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <1148763602....@j33g2000cwa.googlegroups.com>,

Ector <Ec...@mail.ru> writes:
>Please clarify this statement: does it mean that a 2-2 deal in a final
>round will ALWAYS be legal for the player with the best standings
>before the final, since it wound be the same as GW for him?

What's to clarify? The tournament rules are pretty explicit.

The player with the highest total of Victory Points from the
final round only is the tournament winner. The player with the
next highest total of Victory Points from the final round only
is the second place winner, and so on. In the event of a tie,
the players' rankings at the end of the preliminary rounds will
be the deciding tiebreaker.

That is, unlike normal rounds, a tiebreaker is applied, so someone
should always win. Since they win, a deal which causes them to win is
play-to-win.

Theoretically, in a large enough tournament, you could have two players
who were tied on GWs, VPs and TPs. i.e. they were tied when going into
the final. You may well have already had to resolve that tie for the
purposes of who sits where. (In a situation where these are players #4
and #5, you may not have cared since it doesn't make a scrap of
difference.)

It may then be distasteful to have a situation where an already known
arbitrary coin-toss split the two players for positioning in the final,
and will continue to split them if they tie in the final, but this is a
sufficiently remote possibility that I doubt it's ever come up.

--
James Coupe

result in the table split failing anyway.

In tournament play, if I were in a game where 2 people formulated a
table split, I'd try and convince the other two players to help me foil
them, but still, me and the other two players would be much more
concerned about trying to get a VP--I'd be much less likely to give up
a VP in the name of spiting the "table split" pair. On the other hand,
in casual play, if I were in the same situation (players A and B
organize a table split, I'm not one of those players), I'd be far more
likely to not care about the VP I'm losing in the name of making
someone else (i.e. one of player A or B if not both) lose.

> Is it irrational to play for ousting your prey and getting VPs in
> casual games?

No, as that is the assumed goal of the game.

> You could instead attack the player who won the last risk
> game, play to be a absolutely weird Malkavian or throw your cards in
> the air when you start losing.

It is assumed that when we all sit down to play VTES, we are all
playing by the same rules and with the same goal--to try and win by
virtue of the established victory conditions of the game. Otherwise,
there is not reallly any point in playing (well, for me at least) that
particular game.

> Playing is about accepting rules that
> are set by a different world (the game world) and ignoring the rules of
> the real world. If i can accept the rule to oust my prey, i can also
> accept to play to absolutely win, i.e. make the most GWs and if that is
> not possible the most VPs, even by dealing.

Sure. But again, at a certain point, tangible incentives become an
issue. Making a deal to maximize VPs in tournament play has a tangible
incentive (i.e. getting you closer to getting in the finals); making a
deal to do the same thing in casual play lacks the same built in
incentive, and is much more likely to incur the wrath of the other
people at the table, resulting in whatever deal is struck failing or
falling apart, where in tournament play, they would not fail.

Again, look at poker--if I'm playing for actual money, I'll fold like
crazy with a bad opening hand; I play very conservatively when I play
for actual money. If I'm playing for nothing (chips/pennies), I'll play
a much riskier game--I'll go all in just as a bluff, or I'll be much
more likely to play a bad opening hand. In either case, the goal of the
game is the same: maximize income/win the most money, but the context
of the game (real stakes/imaginary stakes) has a significant impact on
how the game is handled.

> BTW, its nice to dicuss game philosophy with you, because you have such
> a different view.

You as well.

-Peter

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <1148918978.0...@j55g2000cwa.googlegroups.com>,

pd...@lightlink.com writes:
>But the inevitable result of "Let's play for a 3/2 split of ambiguity!"
>is someone is deciding to throw the game with no clear legal reason to
>do so.

Well, there are a few issues here.

1a) If the two of us sit next to each other on a five player table, then
it can be indeterminate as to who is getting the win.

1b) If the two of us are cross-table, saying "Let's split it 3-2" does
actually give you an answer, assuming that the intention is to
keep the outcome as 3-2. Let's take the table A-B-C-D-E. A and
D offer a 3-2 deal, but don't specify who gets the win. Okay
then. A gets 2 by ousting B and C, but can't get 3 unless he
ousts D - at which point D either has 1 VP (from E) or 0 VP. So
assuming that 3-2 will be held, A has just agreed to get 2 and D
has agreed to get 3.

2) More generally, it's possible to say to the table in general "Okay,
let's oust the others and then we'll fight it out for the table
win." Which is a perfectly common deal. (Only really works
with a cross-table ally, due to similar restrictions as in 1b.)
It can then be perfectly reasonable for both players to think
they're playing to win, because they both have a deck they think
will oust the other e.g. a weenie deck which thinks it can swarm
through the opponent, versus a deck that's planning to get
Justine out, or an Atonement etc., or some other versatile anti-
weenie tech.

propose to work with 1st strongest. They will likely assume I will
settle for vp's instead of the gamewin. I trade things I need,

that is for a given deck, a rush or two perhaps).

This works best for decks that can help other players very easily, at
little cost to themselves. I've been enjoying using Renewed Vigor to
bargain for the assistance of another player :)

My expectation is, that the deal will be unspecified as to who gets the
2, and who gets the 3, only for an initial period where they are
mutually assisting each other. Then when no other player seems a
serious threat, the friendliness will start to dissolve. Perhaps then
negotiation will open up between the two players trying to determine
who gets the gamewin, or perhaps they will negotiate by bleeding each
other :)

I'm picturing something like, 2 rush decks find themselves predator A
and prey B. They realize that unless they negotiate they will simply
obliterate it each other, handing the grand predator E 2 vps. So they
make a deal to split the table 3-2, but don't specify who gets the 3.
The result would be players C and D get ousted by B. At this point B
has 2 vps and A has zero. If one player is clearly stronger then the
other, perhaps the weaker will see no chance of a gamewin, and accept
the 2 vp position. If it's in contest, then A and B will probably
negotiate in some way. They could talk it out, A could bleed B while B
tries to oust E. Or they might just rush each other into oblivion,
accidentally giving E the gamewin when E ousts both A and B :)

-Matt Kanninen
